title: Ukraine’s internal power struggle: How the war reshaped politics in Kyiv
content:
What unfolded over several weeks in July sheds light on a system of power that, according to Dr Łukasz Adamski, director of the Mieroszewski Centre, today has more in common with the ancient concept of wartime dictatorship than with the constitutional balance between the president and parliament.

The fourth government reshuffle in Kyiv since the outbreak of Russia’s full-scale war was formally presented as a technical overhaul. As part of the reshuffle, Ukraine’s parliament approved the composition of the cabinet at the request of newly appointed Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi. 

On 16 July, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy entrusted the duties of defence minister to the head of the Security Service of Ukraine, General Yevhen Khmara. The new cabinet did not include outgoing Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov – one of the most recognisable technocrats in Ukraine’s wartime government and a politician enjoying enormous public support.

title: Torture, Violence and Death: What Ukrainian POWs Face in Russian Captivity
content:
Despite repeated prisoner exchanges, thousands of Ukrainians remain in Russian captivity, while the number of documented cases of torture and ill-treatment continues to grow. 

“If you were to ask me how severely I was tortured, I would say that on every possible scale, it was at the maximum level,” Ukrainian soldier Khuan Alberto Levya Garsiya said, describing the 1,183 days he spent in Russian captivity.

His testimony, given shortly after the Council meeting, was one of several accounts that together paint a picture of the system Russia has built around Ukrainian prisoners of war and detained civilians.

Garsiya listed the methods of torture he said he had endured with the calm precision of someone who had become familiar enough with them to name them: “daily beatings, electric shocks, exhausting exercises in freezing temperatures of minus 30 degrees Celsius, sexual violence”.

“They did everything that could be done to a person to break them psychologically,” he said.

He was, however, more fortunate than two of his fellow detainees held in detention facilities in the Donetsk region.

“They were beaten to death, and their bodies were sent back to their families in plastic bags,” he added.

title: When Disinformation Takes to the Streets and Causes Harm
content:
Six men and one woman have been remanded in custody for 30 days over an attack on an ambulance in a village in Cluj County, with the woman facing assault charges. Prosecutors said she threw a stone at the ambulance window, injuring the driver.

On Monday morning, the ambulance driver underwent a second surgery after sustaining an eye injury from shards of the shattered window.

The seven suspects stormed an ambulance with clubs, axes and stones after believing false information that had appeared on TikTok. The ambulance had picked up a patient and was taking them to hospital when it was attacked. The viral video invoked the myth of “black ambulances” – a conspiracy theory that has circulated in Romania in the past – which allegedly kidnap children.

Police identified those involved in the incident, which took place on August 8. They are aged between 18 and 44 and come from a village in western Romania.

title: Mark Rutte and the Trump gamble: Saving NATO at what cost?
content:
Since taking over as NATO secretary general, the former Dutch prime minister has cultivated a remarkably warm relationship with Donald Trump. He praises him publicly, credits him with achievements that began long before his return to the White House and rarely challenges him in front of the cameras.

The strategy has produced results. Trump remains engaged with NATO. The alliance has agreed to a dramatic increase in defence spending. And the American president has repeatedly praised Rutte himself.

But there is an increasingly uncomfortable question in European capitals: when does strategic flattery become strategic dependence?

Mark Rutte’s supporters argue that he is doing exactly what the alliance needs in an exceptionally dangerous period. His critics fear that, in trying to keep Trump inside NATO, he may be weakening the very institution he is supposed to lead.

The NATO secretary general is not a commander-in-chief. He does not decide where American troops are deployed, nor can he order European governments to spend more on defence. His principal power is political: persuasion, mediation and consensus-building.

title: EU unemployment remains stable, but 3 million young people are out of work
content:
The labor market and the specter of unemployment are topics that have kept both European governments and ordinary citizens awake at night for decades. Older observers certainly remember the tragic realities of 2013, when the unemployment rate across the European Union reached almost 12 percent, and among young people exceeded an alarming 25 percent. 

At the time, this meant that every fourth young European was unemployed. Somewhat fresher in our memory are the times of the COVID-19 pandemic, when mass lockdowns paralyzed the service sector, driving the unemployment rate in 2020 up to 7.8 percent, with a striking result of 19.2 percent among the youth.

Against the backdrop of these past shocks, today’s situation appears remarkably stable. According to the latest Eurostat data for June 2026, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stood at 6.3 percent in the euro area and exactly 6.0 percent across the European Union — unchanged from a year earlier. Although these figures may look reassuring, they still translate into more than 13.3 million unemployed people across the EU, including over 11 million in the euro area.

title: Will Migrants from Ceuta Flood Europe? The Truth About the Spanish Government’s Decision
content:
Two days at the turn of July and August 2026 were enough for a storm to erupt across the European web, the likes of which the continent had not seen since the great migration crisis a decade ago. When about 60,000 migrants from Morocco attempted to illegally enter Ceuta – a Spanish exclave in North Africa – the internet was flooded with a wave of apocalyptic forecasts. 

According to the most popular narrative, repeated by politicians and anonymous internet users, the left-wing government in Madrid was supposed to welcome all newcomers with open arms, hand them European documents, and open the borders, allowing for an uncontrolled “spillover” of migrants across the entire Schengen area. The problem is that in this virtual scenario, almost nothing matches the facts.

By analyzing the events from the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa step by step, one can see how a coincidence of circumstances, complex laws, and the deliberate activities of smugglers created an ideal environment for disinformation. Here is how the alleged “invasion of Europe” looks when confronted with reality.

title: Inside the Kill Zone: How Drones Are Reshaping the War in Ukraine
content:
Ukrainian and Russian soldiers describe this space as a belt along the line of contact, saturated with reconnaissance equipment, dispersed infantry, isolated trenches, numerous unmanned supply vehicles and small infiltration groups. It is this zone — referred to by military analysts as the “kill zone” — where not only tactical battles are decided, but also the ability to maintain logistics and evacuate the wounded.

“The kill zone is essentially an area of increasing threat, which gradually turns into a danger zone as you move farther away from the front line. This buffer extends 7 to 10 kilometers into each side’s positions,” explains Konrad Muzyka, a military analyst and owner of Rohan Consulting. “The moment any heavy wheeled or tracked vehicle appears in this belt, FPV drones, artillery and other weapons are immediately directed against it.”

title: Modernisation Fund: Green or Gas?
content:
In July 2026, as Europe — the world’s fastest-warming continent — grappled with record-breaking heatwaves threatening public health, infrastructure and economic productivity, the United States’ war with Iran once again exposed the European Union’s vulnerability to volatile imported fossil fuel prices. The spike added €47 billion to the bloc’s fossil fuel import bill in just three months and reignited debate over the future of the European Union’s Emissions Trading System, now emerging as a crucial test of the credibility of the bloc’s climate agenda.

At the heart of that debate is the Modernisation Fund, a large-scale financial instrument financed through the auctioning of carbon emission allowances. During its first five years of operation, from 2021 to 2025, the Fund disbursed more than €20 billion to modernise energy systems and improve energy efficiency in the European Union’s lower-income member states.
